segments.voice: Yesterday: Torah, the handwritten scroll, read to the end and rolled back. Your line was the world's oldest book club. Did you share a line you love? Day twenty-one, the last day of camp one.

This Saturday morning, in a synagogue in Buenos Aires, one in Melbourne, one in a Brooklyn basement and one in a Jerusalem neighborhood, the scroll will be opened, most weeks, to the same place. The same chapters, read in the same week, in the same order, by people who will never meet. Ask a Jewish friend what this week's portion is, and there's a good chance they'll know its name without checking. It's a calendar made of text. And as camp one ends, it's also the road ahead of you on this path. Today: the portion, and where it's about to take us.
screen: `ONE SATURDAY, EVERY CITY.` → `THE SAME CHAPTERS, THE SAME WEEK.` → `A CALENDAR MADE OF TEXT.`

segments.voice: A parsha is a portion. The five books of the Torah are divided into fifty-four of them, and one is read each Sabbath, so the whole scroll is read in about a year. There are fewer Sabbaths than portions in some years, so some weeks two are read together. Each portion is named for one of its first distinctive words. The first is Bereshit, in the beginning. Then Noach, Noah. Then Lech Lecha, go forth, when Abraham leaves home. Jews say the week's name the way other people say the month: that happened the week of Noach. The reading isn't only on Saturday morning. Short pieces are read on Monday and Thursday mornings too, and the Talmud traces that custom back to the time of Moses, so that no one would go three days without Torah, and credits the scribe Ezra with shaping it. The Talmud even suggests a way to study it at home: read the week's portion twice, and once in translation. And here's a detail that says a lot about a scattered people. After some holidays, Israel and the rest of the world fall out of step by a week, and then quietly catch up again. The cycle bends, but it holds. That's why the carry for today is what it is. You don't start the Torah on page one when you're ready. You find out where everyone is, and you step in there. Camp one gave you twenty-one words. Tomorrow camp two begins, the stories, the original serial, and it begins exactly where the cycle does: at the first word, Bereshit.
screen: `FIFTY-FOUR PORTIONS, ONE A WEEK.` · `EACH NAMED FOR AN EARLY WORD.` · `MONDAY, THURSDAY, SABBATH.` · `THE CYCLE BENDS, BUT HOLDS.` · then, large: `STEP IN WHERE EVERYONE IS.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell, to walk back through camp one. Let the words come one by one: shalom, the Shema, Shabbat, the candles, bracha, Genesis one, the Sabbath commandment. Abraham, Jacob, tzedakah, the Exodus, Sinai, the Ten Words, kavanah. Hitbodedut, Yom Kippur, teshuvah, minyan, the mezuzah, Torah, the parsha. Stay with whichever one pulls at you. The bell holds the time.
The parsha. This week's portion, one of fifty-four, read by a whole people in step. Twenty-first word. Camp one, complete.
Your line: join the cycle wherever it is. Today, look up this week's portion and read its first few lines, wherever the year happens to be. Tomorrow, the stories begin. Day twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 21 COUNTS.` → `CAMP ONE COMPLETE.` → `TOMORROW: BEFORE ANYTHING, A VOICE.`

howItsDone: Jews read the weekly Torah portion aloud from the scroll in synagogue on Sabbath mornings, with shorter readings on Monday and Thursday mornings and Sabbath afternoons, and many study it at home during the week.

what it means: a calendar made of text. one of fifty-four portions, read by the whole people in the same week.

what a scholar hears: Bava Kamma 82a traces the Monday and Thursday readings to the prophets of Moses' time and credits Ezra with shaping them; Berakhot 8a: read the portion twice and the Targum once. Israel and the diaspora sometimes run a week apart.

notes: Camp-one close: the practice names all 21 camp-one words; the close points to camp two ('the stories').

Bava Kamma 82a: the prophets of Moses' time instituted Monday/Thursday/Sabbath readings so no three days pass without Torah; Ezra added details (three readers, ten verses, Sabbath afternoon). Script was corrected from 'Ezra instituted it so no three days pass' to reflect this. Confirm.

Hook says congregations everywhere read the same portion; many Reform and some Conservative congregations follow a triennial cycle (a third of each portion), and Israel and the diaspora sometimes differ by a week. Hedged with 'most weeks'; a Keeper may want the triennial cycle mentioned.
'Once in translation' refers to the Targum (Onkelos); simplified. Confirm.
